Newly hatched Cabezon emerge from demersal eggs as yolk-sac larvae measuring 0.585 cm [Lb = 0.585 cm] in total length, a remarkably small initial size for a species that ultimately achieves considerable bulk. During the first days post-eclosion, these prolarvae remain in the interstitial spaces of rocky reef substrate, absorbing endogenous yolk reserves from their prominent yolk sac. Field rearing observations indicate that the period from fertilisation to hatching spans approximately 11 days [ab = approximately 11 days] when water temperatures average 10 °C [T = 10 °C], a developmental duration consistent with the cool-water thermal regime typical of the northeastern Pacific coastal habitats this fish occupies. The lecithotrophic stage persists until the larvae exhaust their yolk supply, at which point mouth opening and retinal differentiation enable the trophic switch to exogenous feeding on copepod nauplii and other small zooplankton. This transition marks a critical bottleneck in early survival, as the small size of these protolarvae makes them vulnerable to both starvation in low-prey environments and predation by gelatinous zooplankton. The initial total length recorded at emergence provides a baseline against which to gauge the extraordinary growth trajectory that carries this sculpin from a millimeter-scale larva to a large-bodied demersal predator.

As juveniles transition to a benthic existence following larval metamorphosis and settlement into rocky intertidal and subtidal habitats, their growth trajectory is heavily influenced by prey availability and thermal conditions. Males of this species achieve a particularly impressive ultimate total length, with the largest documented individuals reaching 99 cm [Li = 99 cm], positioning Cabezon among the more formidable members of the family Cottidae in terms of maximal body size. This asymptotic length is attained only after many years of steady growth, reflecting the protracted life span characteristic of this cold-water fish. The ultimate wet weight associated with such large specimens is equally striking, as fully-grown adults have been recorded at 6800 grams [Wwi = 6800 grams], a mass that concentrates substantial muscular tissue used both for ambush predation and for maintaining position against strong nearshore currents. This heavyweight morphology is supported by a robust skeletal structure and a capacious gut capable of processing large invertebrate prey, including crabs, octopuses, and smaller fishes. The attainment of such body dimensions underscores the species' role as a dominant benthic predator within the kelp forest and rocky reef ecosystems it inhabits along the Pacific coast of North America from northern California to British Columbia.

Sexual maturation in Cabezon is characterized by a notable divergence between the sexes in both the timing and size at which reproductive competence is achieved. Females attain a total length at puberty of 33.7 cm [Lp = 33.7 cm], a size that typically corresponds to the onset of vitellogenesis and the ability to produce viable clutches of demersal eggs. Males, in contrast, undergo the initiation of spermatogenesis and achieve reproductive maturity at a smaller body size, with a total length at puberty of 29.7 cm [Lp = 29.7 cm]. This sexual dimorphism in maturation size is likely linked to the differing energetic demands of reproduction between the sexes: females must allocate substantial resources toward yolk production and the development of large, adhesive egg masses, while males invest more heavily in nest site preparation, courtship, and the defense of spawning territories. Under the thermal conditions characteristic of the species' core range, where bottom temperatures hover around 12 °C [T = 12 °C], females begin their first reproductive events after approximately 657 days since birth [tR = approximately 657 days since birth], while males achieve their first spawning slightly earlier, at roughly 584 days since birth [tR = roughly 584 days since birth]. These ages at first reproduction represent a moderately fast life history schedule for a fish of this ultimate size.

The maximum lifespan documented for Cabezon under natural conditions reaching approximately 4745 days [am = approximately 4745 days] when experienced in habitats with an average temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C], reflects the species' position on the slow end of the life-history continuum for nearshore sculpins. This considerable longevity, equivalent to roughly 13 years, allows individuals multiple reproductive opportunities across several breeding seasons, an iteroparous strategy that buffers against occasional recruitment failures. The prolonged adult phase is supported by a relatively low natural mortality rate once individuals reach the large body sizes that confer protection against most gape-limited predators. Older, larger individuals, particularly those approaching the ultimate total length of 99 cm [Li = 99 cm], exhibit slowed somatic growth as energy is increasingly diverted toward gamete production and nest-guarding behaviors. This life span is notably longer than that of many smaller cottids, which typically complete their life cycles in five to eight years, suggesting that the energetic trade-offs associated with attaining a large body mass and producing sizable benthic egg masses are offset by the benefits of repeated spawning over a decade or more. Such a strategy is consistent with stable, resource-rich environments.

Reproductive ecology in Cabezon features a fascinating reproductive strategy centered on the production of large, adhesive demersal egg masses that are deposited in rocky crevices and actively guarded by the male parent. Field surveys of nesting sites indicate that females produce a single large clutch per breeding season [F_R_i = single large clutch per breeding season], with individual fecundity ranging from approximately 50,000 to 100,000 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 50,000 to 100,000 eggs per clutch] depending on the female's body size. This substantial investment per reproductive event is characteristic of a strategy that prioritizes offspring size and paternal protection over high fecundity and broadcast spawning. The male's nest-guarding behavior, which can last for several weeks until the eggs hatch, represents a significant energetic cost that may limit the number of clutches a single male can successfully tend in a season. The eggs, which are pink to orange in color and measure about 2 mm in diameter, are laid in a cohesive mass that the male aerates by fanning and from which he removes dead or diseased embryos. This combination of large clutch size, single annual reproductive event, and extended paternal care underscores the species' reliance on high per-offspring survival rather than numerical dispersal.
